title: Vindaloo (anglicised)
subtitle: Hot and sour pork curry
excerpt: The British restaurant vindaloo interpretation: pork braised in a fiery sauce of chillies, vinegar, garlic, cumin, and mustard seed. Different from the original Goan carne de vinha d'alhos, but genuinely good in its own right.
sourceNotes: The British 'vindaloo' is a distinct preparation from the original Goan carne de vinha d'alhos. This recipe follows the Anglo-Indian restaurant style. Cross-referenced with Pat Chapman, India: Food & Cooking (2007) for the vinegar-chilli spice base.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes for up to 3 months. Freezing mellows the heat slightly.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well. Excellent the day after.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Marinate the pork for at least 2 hours, ideally overnight. The finished curry improves with resting.

content.text: The anglicised vindaloo is a hot-and-sour curry built on a paste of chillies, vinegar, and spices. The original Goan dish (carne de vinha d'alhos, 'meat in wine and garlic') is a Portuguese-influenced preparation that is milder and more aromatic; the British version evolved in Indian restaurants into something fiercer. This recipe follows the restaurant style with pork shoulder.

items.prepNote: or 1 tbsp hot chilli powder + 1 tbsp sweet paprika

content.text: Blend the garlic, ginger, chilli powder, ground spices, mustard seeds, and vinegar to a smooth paste. Add 2 tablespoons of water if needed to help it blend.
Toss the pork cubes with half the paste and a generous pinch of salt. Marinate in the fridge for at least 2 hours.
Heat the oil in a large casserole over medium-high heat. Brown the marinated pork in batches until coloured on all sides. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, cook the onion over medium heat for 10 minutes until dark golden. Add the remaining paste and cook for 3 minutes, stirring, until fragrant.

Add the tinned tomatoes and 200 ml water. Return the pork. Bring to a simmer, then cook over low heat, covered, for 60 to 75 minutes until the pork is very tender. The sauce should be thick and slightly separated from the oil. Season.

items.symptom: The curry is not hot enough
items.cause: Chilli powder was not potent or quantity insufficient
items.fix: Add more hot chilli powder or a pinch of cayenne. Taste before serving and adjust.

items.symptom: The pork is still tough after 1 hour
items.cause: Not cooked low and slow enough
items.fix: Continue at the lowest possible heat for another 30 minutes. Pork shoulder needs long, gentle cooking.

items.symptom: The sauce lacks the sour vinegar note
items.fix: Add another tablespoon of vinegar at the very end and stir in. Do not further cook after adding.

items.symptom: The oil is not separating from the sauce
items.fix: Remove the lid and cook over medium heat for 10 minutes to reduce and concentrate.

content.text: The British vindaloo has become a cultural institution of a particular kind: the macho curry-house challenge, ordered by people who want the hottest thing on the menu. The original Goan dish from which it descends is nothing like this. Carne de vinha d'alhos (meat in wine and garlic) is a Portuguese-influenced marinade preparation, moderately spiced, eaten by Goan Catholics who adopted it from their Portuguese colonisers. The British restaurant transformation into a fire-bomb dish is a culinary evolution, not a corruption: it is a different dish, with its own tradition and audience.
